chapters.name: Sign Shapes, Colors, and Regulatory Signs
chapters.summary: How the shape and color of a sign tell you what kind of message it gives, and the signs that state rules you must obey.
keyPoints: The eight-sided sign is used only for STOP, and the downward-pointing triangle is used only for YIELD.
Regulatory signs are usually white rectangles with black or red letters and give rules such as speed limits and turn limits.
A red circle with a slash over a symbol means the action shown is not allowed.

chapters.name: Warning, School, Railroad, and Work Zone Signs
chapters.summary: Yellow diamond warning signs, the school and railroad signs, and the orange signs used in construction and maintenance zones.
keyPoints: Most warning signs are yellow with black symbols and are diamond shaped; they tell you about a hazard or change ahead.
The round yellow railroad advance warning sign and the white crossbuck at the tracks tell you a railroad crossing is near.
Orange signs mark construction and maintenance work zones, where fines are higher and speeds are often lowered.

chapters.name: Guide Signs and Route Markers
chapters.summary: Green, blue, and brown guide signs and the shields that mark Interstate, U.S., and state routes.
keyPoints: Green signs give directions and guidance, blue signs show services, and brown signs point to recreation and cultural sites.
Interstate, U.S. highway, Michigan state highway, and county roads each have their own route marker shape.
Guide signs also show freeway exits, the direction to towns, and services such as gas and rest areas.

chapters.name: Traffic Signals, Pavement Markings, and Michigan Lefts
chapters.summary: What each traffic light and arrow means, how to read white and yellow lines, and how to make a Michigan Left.
keyPoints: A flashing red light means stop, then go when it is safe; a flashing yellow light means slow down and go ahead with care.
A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn left only after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.
Yellow lines separate traffic going in opposite directions, and white lines separate lanes going the same way.

chapters.name: Right of Way, Emergency Vehicles, School Buses, and Railroad Crossings
chapters.summary: Who goes first at intersections and roundabouts, and what to do for emergency vehicles, school buses, and trains.
keyPoints: Drivers turning left must yield to oncoming traffic, and drivers must yield to pedestrians in crosswalks.
When a school bus shows flashing red lights, stop at least 20 feet away until the lights stop flashing.
When you must stop for a train, stop no more than 50 feet and no less than 15 feet from the tracks.

chapters.name: Speed Limits, Passing, Turning, and Parking
chapters.summary: Michigan speed limits, when passing is allowed, how to turn and change lanes, and where parking is not allowed.
keyPoints: Unless posted otherwise, the limit is 25 mph in platted subdivisions and 55 mph on other roads; freeways allow up to 70 mph with a 55 mph minimum.
Do not pass within 100 feet of an intersection or railroad crossing, or when your view is blocked within 100 feet of a bridge or tunnel.
Do not park within 15 feet of a fire hydrant, within 20 feet of a marked crosswalk, or within 30 feet of a stop sign or traffic light.

chapters.name: Safe Driving, Sharing the Road, and Emergencies
chapters.summary: Following distance, freeway driving, bad weather, night driving, deer, and sharing the road with trucks, bicycles, and motorcycles.
keyPoints: Leave at least 3 or 4 seconds between you and the vehicle ahead, and more in bad weather.
Give a bicyclist at least 3 feet of space when passing.
If a deer crash cannot be avoided, brake firmly, hold the wheel, and stay in your lane instead of swerving.

chapters.name: Graduated Driver Licensing and Permits
chapters.summary: The driver education segments and the three licensing levels for teens, and the temporary instruction permit for new adult drivers.
keyPoints: A Level 1 Learner's License needs Segment 1 and an age of at least 14 years, 9 months, and allows driving only with a licensed parent, guardian, or designated adult 21 or older.
Before the driving skills test you need 50 hours of supervised driving, including 10 at night, and at least six months with a Level 1 license.
Level 2 drivers may not drive from 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. or carry more than one passenger under 21, with listed exceptions.

chapters.name: Alcohol, Distracted Driving, Seat Belts, and Points
chapters.summary: Drunk and drugged driving laws, implied consent, Michigan's hands-free law, seat belt and child seat rules, and the point system.
keyPoints: Drivers under 21 may not have any bodily alcohol content; a drunk driving charge applies at 0.08 BAC, and a higher penalty applies at 0.17 or more.
Michigan law does not allow drivers to hold or manually use a mobile phone while driving.
Points stay on your driving record for two years from the date of conviction.
